causes: A drop in blood pressure upon standing, often related to dehydration, prolonged bed rest, certain medications, or autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
pathophysiology: Insufficient vasoconstriction/heart-rate compensation when moving from lying or sitting to standing causes transient cerebral hypoperfusion.
diagnosis: Suggested by symptoms of dizziness or faintness specifically on standing, and confirmed with orthostatic blood-pressure measurements taken lying, sitting, and standing.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about timing relative to posture changes, medication history, hydration, and check blood pressure in multiple positions.
consumer_summary: Feeling dizzy or light-headed mainly when you stand up quickly, sometimes with brief loss of balance.

causes: Most commonly benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) from displaced inner-ear crystals, or Meniere's disease.
pathophysiology: Abnormal signals from the vestibular system create a false sensation of motion or spinning, often triggered by head position changes.
diagnosis: Ask about whether the sensation is a true spinning feeling versus general light-headedness, triggers related to head movement, and any associated hearing symptoms.
what_a_doctor_does: Positional testing (e.g. Dix-Hallpike maneuver), hearing assessment, and review of episode duration/frequency.
consumer_summary: A spinning or whirling sensation, sometimes brought on by rolling over in bed or looking up.

causes: Age-related degeneration of the cervical spine discs and joints.
pathophysiology: Degenerative changes can irritate nerves or restrict blood flow contributing to dizziness with neck movement.
diagnosis: History of neck pain/stiffness with dizziness related to neck posture; imaging can confirm degenerative changes.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about neck pain, posture-related triggers, prior neck injury, and perform a neck range-of-motion exam.
consumer_summary: Neck stiffness or soreness along with occasional dizziness, especially after turning your head.

causes: Reduced lactase enzyme activity leading to undigested lactose fermenting in the colon.
pathophysiology: Undigested lactose draws water into the intestine and is fermented by gut bacteria, producing gas and cramping.
diagnosis: Symptom correlation with dairy intake, timing (typically 30 minutes to 2 hours after consuming dairy), and symptom relief on a lactose-free trial.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask specifically about dairy consumption (milk, ice cream, cheese) preceding symptoms and consider a lactose-free trial or hydrogen breath test.
consumer_summary: Stomach cramps, bloating, or loose stools that tend to happen after eating dairy like milk or ice cream.

causes: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter allowing stomach acid to flow back into the esophagus.
pathophysiology: Acid exposure irritates the esophageal lining, producing burning discomfort, often worse when lying down or after large meals.
diagnosis: Symptom pattern related to meals and lying down; trial of acid-suppressing medication; endoscopy in persistent/atypical cases.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about meal timing, lying down after eating, spicy/fatty food triggers, and any alarm symptoms (difficulty swallowing, weight loss).
consumer_summary: A burning feeling in the chest or throat, often after eating or when lying down.

causes: Not fully understood; associated with gut-brain axis dysregulation, stress, and altered gut motility/sensitivity.
pathophysiology: Visceral hypersensitivity and abnormal motility produce recurrent pain typically relieved by defecation.
diagnosis: Recurrent abdominal pain associated with a change in stool frequency or form, in the absence of alarm features.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about pain-defecation relationship, stress triggers, and screen for alarm symptoms warranting further workup.
consumer_summary: Ongoing stomach cramping and irregular bowel habits, often linked to stress or certain foods, without a clear single trigger.

causes: IgE-mediated allergic reaction to airborne allergens such as dust mites, pollen, or pet dander.
pathophysiology: Allergen exposure triggers histamine release causing nasal mucosal swelling, clear rhinorrhea, and itching.
diagnosis: Clear, thin nasal discharge with itching and sneezing, often seasonal or with specific environmental triggers.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about discharge color/consistency, itching in nose/eyes/throat, and exposure to dust, pets, or seasonal pollen.
consumer_summary: A stuffy or runny nose with clear, watery discharge, itching, and sneezing, often triggered by dust, pollen, or pets.

causes: Viral or bacterial infection causing inflammation of the sinus lining, often following a cold.
pathophysiology: Inflammation blocks sinus drainage, leading to pressure, pain, and thickened discharge.
diagnosis: Facial pain/pressure with thick, often discolored nasal discharge, sometimes with fever, lasting more than a week.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about discharge color, facial pain location, duration of symptoms, and recent upper-respiratory infection.
consumer_summary: Nasal blockage with thick, colored mucus, facial pressure or pain, sometimes with fever.

causes: Non-allergic nasal hyperreactivity triggered by irritants, temperature change, or strong odors rather than an immune allergic response.
pathophysiology: Autonomic nervous system overreaction to non-allergic triggers causes nasal blood vessel dilation and congestion.
diagnosis: Similar symptoms to allergic rhinitis but without a clear allergen trigger and typically negative allergy testing.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about specific triggers (temperature changes, strong smells, spicy food) and rule out allergic causes.
consumer_summary: Stuffy or runny nose triggered by things like weather changes, strong smells, or spicy food rather than allergies.

causes: Prolonged use of over-the-counter nasal decongestant sprays beyond a few days.
pathophysiology: Repeated vasoconstriction leads to rebound vasodilation and worsening congestion once the medication wears off.
diagnosis: History of extended nasal decongestant spray use with worsening congestion despite continued or increased use.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask specifically about over-the-counter nasal spray use and duration.
consumer_summary: Nasal stuffiness that keeps coming back or gets worse despite using decongestant nasal sprays regularly.

causes: Hormonal imbalance involving elevated androgens and insulin resistance.
pathophysiology: Disrupted ovulation and elevated androgens lead to irregular cycles and associated skin/hair changes.
diagnosis: Combination of irregular periods, clinical or biochemical signs of excess androgens, and/or ultrasound findings.
what_a_doctor_does: Ask about menstrual regularity, hair growth pattern, acne, and family history; may order hormone panels and pelvic ultrasound.
consumer_summary: Irregular periods along with symptoms like acne or extra hair growth, related to a hormone imbalance.
